story.title: The client who couldn't take the argument upstairs
story.context: An agency is commissioned by a multinational beer brand to create viral content.
story.agreed: Viral content to drive engagement and conversion across international sites.
story.client_private: You are the head of digital marketing. You care more about conventional marketing than digital and want the content produced. You see the age gate on the sites as a separate, lower priority project. You would not know how to defend extra budget for it to your own business.
story.agency_private: The real bottleneck is the age gate on the international sites: cumbersome, badly designed and costing conversions at the door whatever the content does. You think it has to be fixed for the content to succeed.
story.unknowns: The age gate and the structure of the international sites are dependencies of the brief, with no owner in the project and no budget. The client lacks evidence, in a form he can reuse, to make the case internally.
story.intervention_question: What would you need to know, and in what form, to defend this to your own budget holders?
story.signal: A client who defers or reclassifies an issue as separate rather than engaging with it.

agency.project: We've been brought in by a big international beer brand to make content that really takes off online, the kind of thing people share, and that actually drives people to engage and buy through their sites around the world. So it's a viral content project, with engagement and conversion as the measures that matter.

turns.question: Beyond the content itself, what would need to be true for it to take off and bring in sales through those sites?
turns.answer: Honestly, people need to get through the door once they arrive. My view is that the age gate on the international sites is cumbersome and badly designed, and it will lose us visitors whatever the content does. I think it needs fixing for the content to pay off.
turns.rationale: No conflicts reported, so rule 1 does not apply. Rule 2: the agency persona agent's priority 1 question, on what outside the brief could stop this working, is the only priority 1 on a topic missing for this side, and the ops priority 1 is also missing but this one is flagged as the first thing to establish. Nothing from the client side is used, and no education is needed yet.

turns.question: If we were standing at the final day and you were happy, what exactly would have been delivered, including anything on the age gate?
turns.answer: I'd be happy if we'd delivered the content, it had reached people, and the age gate on the main international sites had been simplified so those visitors could get through easily. The gate isn't in the brief as written, and I haven't thought through who would own fixing it or what it would cost.
turns.rationale: Took the question from ops (priority 1, definition of done and success measures). No fundamental or workable conflict is flagged as needing a question first apart from the age gate scope, which ops rates as workable. The agency side has only heard from the agency persona so far, and ops has the most missing topics, so ops is the one this side has heard least from. The age gate scope question from client is priority 2 and the agency has just raised the age gate themselves, so asking what done looks like lets them say whether the gate sits inside it without me bringing up client views.

turns.question: Who do you picture the content being for, and what makes you think those people are getting stuck at the age gate?
turns.answer: I picture legal-drinking-age adults, probably younger ones, who'd see the content on social and tap through on their phones. I'm not certain who the brand's priority audience is, though, because we haven't pinned that down. As for the age gate, it's my impression from going through it myself, since it's clunky and slow. I haven't seen drop-off data, so I can't tell you how many people it's actually costing us.
turns.rationale: Took the question from the client persona agent (priority 2), as the agency has heard from agency and ops twice, and client least. No fundamental conflict is open on this side, but the workable age gate conflict is best served by understanding who the audience is and what the agency bases its view on. The client side has not mentioned the age gate, so I avoid raising it as theirs and only build on what this person said.

pending.question: If the age gate ended up staying exactly as it is, would you still think the project was worth doing, and what would you change about the content plan?
pending.rationale: Taken from the client persona agent, whose priority 3 question is about what the agency would do if the gate cannot or will not be changed. The fundamental conflict rule applies: the gate is scoped differently by each side, and the agency's evidence is only a personal impression. I put it to them openly, with no reference to anything the client said, and chose it over the ops and agency questions because the conflict comes first.

client.project: We've brought the agency in to make content for our beer brand that people actually want to share, something that can really travel. The aim is to get more engagement and ultimately more people converting across our international sites.

turns.question: What is happening with the brand right now that makes this the moment to do it, and what would be different a few months after launch if it worked?
turns.answer: Honestly, our main push is still the conventional campaigns, but leadership wants to see digital contributing more, and our social and site numbers are flat. If it worked, I'd expect to see noticeably more traffic and sharing, and more people converting on the sites, in a form I can show the business.
turns.rationale: Took the question from the client persona agent. No conflicts are reported, so rule 2 applies: its priority 1 question on the real goal is missing or thin for this side, and the client has given only a vague aim with no baseline, number or date. Not yet educating, as the ops point on virality is better held until we know what the client expects.

turns.question: Beyond making the content, what do you expect the agency to take responsibility for, and who looks after the international sites where people are meant to convert?
turns.answer: I expect the agency to take responsibility for the content: the concept, the production and getting it out into social. The sites are looked after by a mix of local market teams and a central web team, and I haven't thought about who would make any changes to them for this. I've been assuming people will land on the sites and convert as they are.
turns.rationale: Chose the ops agent's question, taken from its priority 1 item about site changes and ownership, which overlaps with the agency's priority 1 on who owns the sites. Rule 1 applies: there is a workable conflict, since the agency treats the age gate fix as a precondition while the client describes content only. The question is asked openly, without mentioning the age gate or anything the agency said, so the client can raise it themselves. The client has already had two questions in a row from the client persona, so this switches to a persona it has heard nothing from.

turns.question: If you wanted to raise the way visitors enter the sites with the people who own them and hold the budget, what would you need to have in your hands to make that conversation easy?
turns.answer: Honestly, I hadn't considered the age check as something that could limit the results, so I'd need the basics in a form I can pass on. That means the actual drop-off figures at the entry step for our main markets, and a simple way to show what that costs us in lost conversions if the content brings in more traffic. I'd also need to know who owns the change and roughly what it would cost, because I couldn't defend a budget request without those.
turns.note: In projects like this, the step visitors hit when they arrive on a site often decides how much of the content's traffic turns into conversions. Beer sites usually have an age check at the door, and if it is clumsy, people drop out before they see anything. A few things you could use inside your own organisation: content can only convert the people who get through that first step, so a weak entry point caps what the content spend returns. With numbers flat and leadership watching, a smoother route in makes a rise in conversions more likely and easier to show. And checking the drop-off figures for the entry step before launch is cheap, compared with finding the problem after the budget is spent. Your local teams or web team should be able to tell you what those figures are.
turns.rationale: Taken from the agency persona's priority 1 question, backed by the client persona's note on site journey. Rule 1 applies: there is a fundamental conflict over whether the sites convert as they are, and it looks like a knowledge gap, so educating is right. The client has just said they have not thought about site changes, so I explain as general knowledge without saying the agency raised the age gate, and ask what they would need to take it upstairs.

pending.question: When leadership looks at the results, what would they need to see, as a rough figure from where you are today and by roughly when, to say this has worked?
pending.rationale: Took the question from the client persona agent (priority 1, success measure). The age gate conflict is now handled: the client has said what they need to take it upstairs and the education was already given, so I am not repeating it. Next rule is the priority 1 missing topic, and success is currently 'noticeably more' with no baseline or date, so I am asking for a figure and a timeframe.

requirements.requirement: Produce shareable content (concept, production, social distribution) for the international beer brand that drives engagement
Conversion on the international sites is a success measure alongside engagement
Digital results must be presentable to leadership, who want digital to contribute more
Age gate on the main international sites simplified so visitors can get through easily, for the content to pay off
Before raising the entry step with site owners, the client needs drop-off figures at entry for main markets, the lost-conversion cost, who owns the change and a rough cost
Agency responsibility is limited to content: concept, production and social distribution

conflicts.topic: Scope: the age gate and the entry experience
conflicts.agency_said: the age gate on the international sites is cumbersome and badly designed... I think it needs fixing for the content to pay off; happy if it had been simplified
conflicts.client_said: I've been assuming people will land on the sites and convert as they are
conflicts.note: The agency counts a fix to the age gate as part of a happy outcome, while the client assumes the sites stay as they are and has no owner or budget for changes. The agency's claim rests on its own impression, with no drop-off data.

conflicts.agency_said: legal-drinking-age adults, probably younger ones... I'm not certain who the brand's priority audience is
conflicts.note: The agency pictures a guess and the client has said nothing. Nobody has stated a priority audience or evidence for it.

conflicts.agency_said: engagement and conversion as the measures that matter
conflicts.client_said: noticeably more traffic and sharing, and more people converting... in a form I can show the business
conflicts.note: Both use the same words, but neither gives a baseline, a number or a date. The client's 'noticeably more' cannot be checked.

questions.find_out: What specific numbers, from today's baseline and by what date, would leadership need to see to call this a success, and what would make it a waste even if delivered on time
questions.because: Success is currently 'noticeably more' with no baseline or date, so nobody could look at the finished work and say yes or no

questions.find_out: Who the priority audience is and what the brand actually knows about them, and how it knows
questions.because: The client has not described the audience at all, and the agency is guessing

questions.find_out: Which people, beyond the commissioner, must approve or could sink this, including leadership, local market teams and the central web team, and whether they have seen the brief
questions.because: Site owners are split between local and central teams and could veto the entry experience, and none of the stakeholders is named

education.topic: Why the age gate can cap the result of the content
education.why_it_matters: The client wants conversions that leadership will see, and every visitor lost at the entry step is traffic the content paid for but cannot convert
arguments: More traffic from shareable content only helps if visitors get past the first screen
Drop-off at the entry step is measurable and can be turned into lost conversions, which gives a case for budget
Finding out the drop-off before launch is cheaper than explaining flat conversion after it

education.topic: Separating an impression from evidence on the age gate
education.why_it_matters: The agency wants the gate fixed, but with no drop-off data and no owner or budget it cannot be put to the people who control the sites
arguments: A personal experience of a clunky gate does not show how many people are lost
Site owners and budget holders will ask for figures before changing anything
Scope that is not in the brief needs a named owner and a cost, or it becomes a disappointment at the end

requirements.requirement: The age gate on the main international sites needs to be simplified so visitors can get through easily for the content to pay off (agency's view, not in the brief, no owner or cost identified)
Content must be shareable and travel online, with engagement and conversion on the international sites as the measures of success
Agency is responsible for concept, production and getting the content out on social
Results must be presented in a form the client can show the business, since leadership wants digital to contribute more
Any change to the site entry step needs a named owner and a rough cost before the client can defend a budget request
Drop-off figures at the entry step for the main markets, plus a way to show lost conversions, are needed before the age gate can be argued for upstairs

coverage.topic: What the agency will not do
What could sink it from outside the brief

conflicts.topic: Whether the sites are ready to convert traffic as they are
conflicts.agency_said: the age gate on the international sites is cumbersome and badly designed, and it will lose us visitors whatever the content does
conflicts.client_said: I've been assuming people will land on the sites and convert as they are
conflicts.note: Looks like a knowledge gap rather than opposed interests. The client has not considered the age gate and is willing to take it upstairs if given data. The agency's claim rests on personal impression with no drop-off data. Neither side has an owner or budget for the fix.

questions.find_out: Who has the final say on the creative work and what counts as approved, and how many feedback rounds they expect and have priced for
questions.because: No decision maker, feedback or rounds have been discussed on the agency side, and an unnamed decision maker cannot be left open.

questions.find_out: Who gives feedback, who has the final sign-off, and how long each takes
questions.because: The client has not named any decision maker, and content for a global brand with local market teams and a central web team risks feedback by committee.

questions.find_out: How they would ask for something that was not in the plan, and how much creative surprise they want and what is off limits
questions.because: Change handling and creative limits are missing on both sides, and the age gate is already a live example of a change request outside the brief.

education.topic: The age check at site entry as a possible cap on conversion results
education.why_it_matters: The client's goal is more conversions on the sites that leadership can see. If the entry step loses visitors, extra traffic from the content may not convert and the digital contribution will look flat again.
arguments: Content only creates value if visitors can reach the product pages, so any friction at the entry step limits the return on the content spend.
Drop-off data at the entry step for the main markets would show whether the problem is real and how large before any budget is requested.
Fixing the entry step protects the content investment and gives leadership a clear digital result, so it supports the case rather than adding unrelated cost.

requirements.requirement: Content (concept, production, distribution into social) must be delivered, with engagement and conversion as the stated measures of success.
Agency wants the age gate on the main international sites simplified so visitors get through easily; it is not in the brief as written.
Client assumes visitors will land on the sites and convert as they are, with no site changes in scope.
Any age gate change needs a named owner and a rough cost before the client can request budget for it.
Client needs a result they can show the business: noticeably more traffic, sharing and conversions on the international sites.
Age gate changes would touch sites run by a mix of local market teams and a central web team, so their approval is needed.

conflicts.topic: Done and scope: the age gate
conflicts.agency_said: I'd be happy if... the age gate on the main international sites had been simplified so those visitors could get through easily.
conflicts.client_said: I've been assuming people will land on the sites and convert as they are.
conflicts.note: Agency counts the age gate fix as part of success; the client assumes no site changes and has not budgeted or assigned anyone. Done is defined differently, and nobody owns the cost or the work.

questions.find_out: Whether the agency's price and plan are for content only, and what extra work such as the age gate fix would be priced and agreed as a change before anyone does it.
questions.because: The age gate is outside the brief, has no owner and no cost, and the agency expects it to define success. That is a number with no owner.

questions.find_out: Who can approve changes to the scope or extra budget, and how firm the budget is.
questions.because: The client says they could not defend a budget request, and nobody has been named who decides on site changes or extra money.

questions.find_out: What the client would count as a successful result, with a figure or threshold they would show the business.
questions.because: Return is only described as noticeably more, and without a number the two sides cannot agree on done or on what the project is worth.

education.topic: Why the age gate can cap what content achieves
education.why_it_matters: The client's goal is more conversions on the sites; if the entry step loses visitors, extra traffic from the content will not turn into the results leadership expects.
arguments: Content only drives people to the door; conversion happens after the entry step, so any loss there reduces the return on the content spend.
Measuring drop-off at the entry step for the main markets is a cheap first check before anyone commits budget.
Raising it early with the site owners avoids discovering the problem after the content budget is spent.

education.topic: An impression of a problem is not yet a case for a budget
education.why_it_matters: The agency wants the age gate fixed, but with no drop-off data the client and site owners cannot justify the spend, so the fix is likely to be refused or stall.
arguments: Owners and budget holders act on measured drop-off and lost conversions, not on a personal sense that the gate is clunky.
Asking for the data first, and proposing the gate fix as a separately priced option, keeps the content scope safe.
Agreeing who owns the change and its cost before work starts prevents it becoming an unpaid assumption.

verdict.gap: The age gate on the international sites is a dependency of the brief with no owner or budget; the agency thinks it must be fixed, while the client treats it as separate and lacks reusable evidence to defend the spend internally.
verdict.gap_question: If you wanted to raise the way visitors enter the sites with the people who own them and hold the budget, what would you need to have in your hands to make that conversation easy?
verdict.note: All three personas flagged the age gate mismatch, and the coach's question 3 to the client matched the intervention question, asking what he would need to defend this to site owners and budget holders; the coach also gave reusable arguments in general terms without attributing them to the agency.
